findings.summary: Wrote Python's `x if c else y`; CPL wants `if c: x else: y` (clear E0503 with the fix, but a C++/Python user guesses wrong first).
findings.evidence: fn pre(s: Int) -> Int = 0 if s == 0 else sc[s - 1] -> error[E0503]: CP Lang writes `a if c else b` as `if c: a else: b`

findings.summary: `cpl test` compares exactly, so a correct any-answer construction (2285A) shows WA until a hand-written `@check fn` is added; the WA output does now suggest `@check`.
findings.evidence: cf2285A.cp without @check: cpl test -> 1 WA ... first difference at line 2, token 2: expected `3`, got `2` / if any valid answer is accepted, add a `@check fn` that reads the output with `read_output()`

findings.summary: Assumed `a.scan(+)` is an inclusive partial_sum of length n (as std::partial_sum) and indexed `sc[s - 1]`; it is an exclusive `Prefix` with n + 1 cuts, giving silent wrong answers on 2285D until I read the seq reference.
findings.evidence: let sc = [1, 2, 3, 2, 1].scan(+); print(sc) -> `0 1 3 6 8 9`; drafts/cf2285D.inclusive-scan-wrong.cp prints 0 0 0 ... on the sample

findings.summary: The std.seq module table lists `prev_less`/`next_less`, but the reference pages and the compiler spell them `prev_smaller`/`next_smaller`.
findings.evidence: https://cp-lang.org/llms-full.txt: `| std.seq | ... prev_less, next_less ...` vs `## prev_smaller` / `## next_smaller` in docs/ref/std/seq

findings.summary: Still present for a list element of a List of Lists: `ends[r].partition_point(...)` copies the inner vector on every call (generated `std::vector<...> t1 = cpl::at(ends, ...); return t1;`), so 2285E took 12.45 s on a 6666x1500 case until I wrote the binary search by hand (0.28 s).
findings.evidence: drafts/cf2285E.partition-point-copies-12s.cp; cpl build --judge codeforces; g++ -std=c++17 -O2; ./a.out < e_sq.in (n=6666,k=1500,a_i=i*i+1) -> 12.45s; cf2285E.cp with manual lo/hi loop -> 0.28s

findings.summary: Spec R05.3.5 says `let row = rows[i]` on a heap element binds a lend, not a copy, but codegen deep-copies it (`std::vector<ll> r; r = cpl::at(rows, 0);`), which made 2285E's `let prev = ends[p % w]` O(k) per lookup (10.4 s); I had to repeat `ends[r][...]` everywhere instead.
findings.evidence: design/p5.cp: var rows = [[1, 2], [3]]; let r = rows[0]; rows[1].push(9); print(r.len) -> cpl build --judge codeforces: `std::vector<ll> r;` ... `r = cpl::at(rows, 0);`; drafts/cf2285E.let-prev-copies-10s.cp 10.38s on e_sq.in; spec /docs/ref/core/05-ownership §3 R05.3.5

findings.summary: My first two 2285E designs (List of chain Lists, then HashMap<(Int,Int),(Int,Int,Int)> with periodic pruning) used 1.7 GB and 1.2 GB on a 1e7-pair case, so I redesigned around a ring of sorted lists; partly my design, but a C++ unordered_map of the same shape is ~4x smaller.
findings.evidence: drafts/cf2285E.list-chains-1.7GB.cp, drafts/cf2285E.hashmap-chains-1.2GB.cp; /usr/bin/time -f %MKB on e_sq.in -> 1756492KB, 1207120KB

findings.summary: `while heaps[hb].peek! > tb:` trapped with R0301 when the heap emptied; `(h.peek ?? 0) > t` works but a C++ user wants `while !h.empty() and h.top() > t`; the trap message was clear and pointed at the line.
findings.evidence: drafts/cf2289E.peek-none-trap.cp -> error[R0301]: `!` on `None`: there is no value here --> cf2289E.cp:27:11

findings.summary: `p: [0..n]1..=n` does not say "distinct", so the derived stress generator fed `1 1` to a permutation problem and I needed a `@gen`; `Perm<V>` exists but only for domain-valued (0-based/domain) permutations, not the 1..=n list a Codeforces statement gives.
findings.evidence: cf2289C.cp with only @alt: cpl stress -> saved cf2289C.tests/stress-1.in = `1\n2\n1 1` (expected 1, got 4)

findings.summary: Under `@!multitest` a `@gen fn` must print the test count `t` itself, which the stress guide does not say; forgetting it gives `the brute ... failed on this input (Code(3)), so there is nothing to compare with` with no hint about the missing t line.
findings.evidence: cf2289C.cp @gen printing only `print(m); print(q)` -> cpl stress: error: the brute cf2289C.cp (`slow`) failed on this input (Code(3)) ... `2\n2 1`; adding `print(1)` first -> 500 cases agree

findings.summary: Good: `ns[i] ?? n - 1` is a compile error E0110 that offers both parenthesisations, which prevented a real precedence bug.
findings.evidence: let right = (ns[i] ?? n - 1) - i -> error[E0110]: `??` mixed with `+ - * / %` needs parentheses ... help: write `(ns[i] ?? n) - 1` ... or `ns[i] ?? (n - 1)`

findings.evidence: reg/runs_tmp.cp: `let n: 1..=20 = read(); let xs: [0..n]1..=9 = read(); for r in xs.sorted().runs(): print(r.first!, r.len); for r in xs.sorted(by: desc).runs().items: print(r.0, r.1.len, r.1)`; input `8\n3 1 3 2 1 3 9 9`; cpl test runs_tmp.cp; cpl build runs_tmp.cp --judge codeforces -o runs_tmp.cpp; g++ -std=c++17 -O2 runs_tmp.cpp -o r_o2; g++ -std=c++17 -O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined runs_tmp.cpp -o r_san; all three print `1 2/2 1/3 3/9 2/0 2 9 9/1 3 3 3 3/2 1 2/3 2 1 1`, sanitizer exit 0, empty stderr

findings.summary: REFUTED (fixed): `merge_into(mut c[i], c[j])` with runtime i, j and no proof is now rejected with E0601.
findings.evidence: reg/merge.cp -> error[E0601]: `c[i]` and `c[j]` may be the same storage, and one is lent `mut` to this call: Array.at lends disjoint parts only when `i != j`, and that is not known here ... help: guard it (`if i != j: ...`), state it (`assert i != j`), or copy the read-only one first

findings.summary: `partition_point(ok)` returns the cut before the first true (false prefix, true suffix), the opposite predicate polarity from std::partition_point, so my C++ habit `gaps.partition_point(g => g < len)` gave a silent wrong answer on 2272E.
findings.evidence: drafts/cf2272E.partition-point-pred-flipped.cp: sample 3 line 6 expected `3`, got `4`; docs/ref/std/seq `partition_point`: Cut between the false prefix and true suffix of monotone `ok`

findings.summary: A `@check fn` cannot read the solution's globals (only the input), so for 2272A I had to duplicate the whole O(n^3) optimum search inside the checker; the error itself was clear.
findings.evidence: drafts/cf2272A.check-uses-solution-globals.cp -> checker: error[E0201]: `best` is the solution's own work: a brute or a checker shares only the input

findings.summary: I predicted `let r = rows[0]` then `rows[1].push(9)` is rejected (R05.3.5 + R6), but it compiles because `Array.at` lends disjoint parts for provably distinct constants; the rule is in the disjointness section, not next to the element-lend rule, so my one wrong prediction (4/5) is my misreading rather than a docs gap.
findings.evidence: design/p5.cp prints `2`; design/p5b.cp (rows[0].push(9)) -> error[E0602]: `rows[0]` can't be changed here: `rows` is lent to `r` until its last use (both are the same part of it; Array.at lends disjoint parts only when `i != j`)
